questions.qtext:
Consider the implementation of a stack of which is based on dynamic array allocation using malloc in C programming. This implementation allows us to push more elements than the current array capacity. It works as follows.

Suppose the array is full, then to push the next element we first allocate a new array of larger size using malloc, copy all elements to the new array, and free up the old array memory.

When a dynamic array-based stack becomes full, you increase the array size by the following sequence $k, 2 k, 3 k, 4 k, \dots$ for some positive constant $k$. Which means the first time we increase the size by $k$, next time by $2 k$, and so on.

If you have an empty stack that uses an array whose initial size is $k$, and you perform $n$ pushes (assume that $n>k)$. What is the total cost complexity of executing n push operations?
Let cost of expanding from $k$ to $2 k$ has $2 k$ cost, similarly cost of expanding from $2 k$ to $3 k$ has $3 k$ cost.
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 42)

Answer is Option A

Source solution 2 (score: 22)
$\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor$ resizes are required.

Given the cost of expanding from $k$ to $2 k$ has $2 k$ cost. To perform $\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor$ resizes has cost,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Cost } &=2 k+3 k+\ldots+\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor+1\right) k \\
&=2 k+3 k+\ldots+N k \\
&=\left(\frac{N(N+1)}{2}-1\right) k \\
&=O\left(N^{2} k\right) \\
&=O\left(\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}} k\right) \\
&=O\left(\frac{n^{2}}{k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Here, Overall Time Complexity = Push Cost + Expansion Cost

Push Cost: There are n elements, and to push those n elements, it is just O(n)

Expansion Cost: Initial stack size is k. (Think as like, when do we need expansion)

1) When we push the (k+1)th element, 1st expansion(k to 2k) occurs = 2k (given)

2) When we push the (2k+1)th element, 2nd expansion(2k to 3k) occurs = 3k

.

3) When we push the (mk+1)th element, m'th expansion(mk to (m+1)k) occurs = (m+1)k

We can assume that the size (m+1)k is sufficient to contain the n elements.

∴ (m+1)k ≥ n ⇒ m ≈ $n/k$

Total expansion Cost = 2k + 3k + ...+ (m+1)k

= k (2 + 3 + .. + (m+1))

= k $(((m+1)(m+2)/2) - 1)$

≈ k ($m^2$)

= k ($n^2/k^2$)

= $n^2/k$

Overall Time Complexity = O(n) + O($n^2/k$) = O($n^2/k$)

Option: A

Source solution 6 (score: 0)

Concept:

This asks for the cost complexity of a dynamic stack that grows by a fixed constant $k$ (Arithmetic Progression) rather than doubling (Geometric Progression).

Calculation:

  1. Expansions: The stack expands when it hits sizes $k, 2k, 3k, \dots$.

  2. Number of Expansions: For $n$ elements, we need roughly $n/k$ expansions. Let $m = n/k$.

  3. Cost of Expansions:

    • 1st expansion ($k \to 2k$): Cost $2k$

    • 2nd expansion ($2k \to 3k$): Cost $3k$

    • ...

    • $m$-th expansion: Cost $mk$

  4. Total Expansion Cost:

    $$\text{Sum} = 2k + 3k + \dots + mk = k \times (2 + 3 + \dots + n/k)$$

    This is an arithmetic series sum, which is roughly proportional to the square of the number of terms.

    $$\text{Sum} \approx k \times \frac{(n/k)^2}{2} = k \times \frac{n^2}{2k^2} = \frac{n^2}{2k}$$

  5. Complexity:

    The expansion cost dominates the simple push cost ($n$).

    Total Cost = $O(n^2/k)$.

Correct Option:

A. O(n²/k)

questions.qtext:
Consider the memory allocation of $\mathrm{M}$ blocks.

Stack$1$ growing from block $0$ up toward block $\mathrm{M} - 1$ and Stack$2$ growing from block $\mathrm{M}-1$ down to block $0.$

Let Top$1$ (initialized to $-1)$ and Top$2\; ($ initialized to $\mathrm{M})$ be the tops of the stacks. For example, after $2$ calls to PushStack$1$ (data) that allocates elements in Stack$1$ followed by $1$ call to PushStack$2$ (data) that allocates elements in Stack$2,$ the memory that was initially all free blocks now has $3$ allocated blocks as per the figure:

If Stack$1$ was replaced by a circular queue with Front and Rear pointers, then which of the following is true regarding memory utilization?

options.text: you may not be able to add/push into the stack even when there are some free blocks in the memory.
you may not be able to add/enqueue into the queue even when there are some free blocks in the memory.
Stack and queue both can be implemented with efficient memory utilization.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 20)

There are total $M$ blocks.

Suppose –

  • We push $\frac{M}{2}$ elements in stack which grows from rightmost end.
  • We enqueue $\frac{M}{2}$ elements in queue.

$\implies$ Now, front will point to $0^{th}$ block, rear will point to $(\frac{M}{2})^{th}$ block and top will point to $(\frac{M}{2})^{th}$ block.

Now, all $M$ blocks are filled.

Suppose –

  • We dequeue some elements from queue. Lets say $5$ elements.

$\implies$ Now, front will point to $6^{th}$ block, rear will point to $(\frac{M}{2})^{th}$ block and top will point to $(\frac{M}{2})^{th}$ block.

$\implies$ We’ve $5$ blocks free but still we cannot push elements in stack in this current state.

But we can do little readjustments in the queue and then every/all free memory blocks can be utilized by the stack.

Suppose –

  • We push $\frac{M}{2}$ elements in stack which grows from rightmost end.
  • We enqueue $\frac{M}{2}$ elements in queue.

$\implies$ Now, front will point to $0^{th}$ block, rear will point to $(\frac{M}{2})^{th}$ block and top will point to $(\frac{M}{2})^{th}$ block.

Now, all $M$ blocks are filled.

Suppose –

  • We dequeue some elements from queue. Lets say $10$ elements.
  • We enqueue some elements in queue. Lets say $10$ elements.
  • We pop some elements from stack. Lets say $10$ elements.

$\implies$ Now, front will point to $11^{th}$ block, rear will point to $10^{th}$ block and top will point to $(\frac{M}{2} + 10)^{th}$ block.

$\implies$ We’ve $10$ blocks free but we cannot enqueue in the queue in this current state.

But we can do little readjustments in the queue and then every/all free memory blocks can be utilized by the queue.

Answer :- A, B (If there is time constraint on doing $push()$ and $enqueue()$ in $O(1)$)

$or$

Answer :- C (In worst case, readjustments will take $O(M)$ time)

Source solution 4 (score: 2)

Analysis:

This question explores memory fragmentation when mixing different data structure implementations in a shared memory space.

  • Original Setup: Two stacks grow towards each other. This is highly efficient because they consume continuous free space from opposite ends. They only clash when the total memory M is completely full.

  • New Setup: Stack1 is replaced by a Circular Queue.

    • A stack is "anchored" at one end and grows contiguously.

    • A circular queue "crawls" through memory. As you enqueue, the Rear pointer moves forward. As you dequeue, the Front pointer moves forward.

  • The Problem: Imagine the Queue has moved towards the middle of the array (e.g., indices 30 to 40). This leaves free space at the bottom (indices 0 to 29). The Stack grows downwards from the top (index M-1). If the Stack grows enough to hit the Queue's Rear (at index 40), it cannot grow further. However, there is still plenty of free memory at indices 0-29. Because a standard stack requires contiguous memory, it cannot "skip" the queue to use that free space.

Conclusion:

You end up with a situation where the Stack is blocked from growing, even though there are free blocks available elsewhere in memory (specifically, behind the Queue).

Correct Option:

A. you may not be able to add/push into the stack even when there are some free blocks in the memory.

Source solution 5 (score: 1)

AI Answer -


Based on the analysis of memory management and data structure properties, the correct answer is A.

Here is the detailed analysis of why this happens.

1. Understanding the "Efficient" Case (Two Stacks)

In the original image (Figure i), two stacks share an array.

  • Stack 1 grows from Left to Right.

  • Stack 2 grows from Right to Left.

  • Why is this efficient? The free space is always one continuous block in the middle. Overflow only happens when Top1 meets Top2. As long as the total number of elements $< M$, you can always push to either stack. There is zero fragmentation.

2. The Problem with Replacing Stack 1 with a Circular Queue

A Circular Queue behaves differently from a Stack.

  • A Stack is "anchored" at one end (index 0 or $M$).

  • A Queue "crawls" through memory. As you Enqueue and Dequeue, the Front and Rear pointers both move to the right. The active data window shifts.

This shifting creates Fragmentation.

Let's look at a concrete example to prove Option A:

Imagine the array size $M = 10$ (Indices 0 to 9).

  1. Stack 2 (growing from right) has data at indices 9, 8, 7, 6. (Top2 is at 6).

  2. The Queue (replacing Stack 1) has performed several operations. Currently, it occupies indices 3, 4, 5. (Front=3, Rear=5).

  3. The Free Blocks: Indices 0, 1, 2 are free. (The Queue moved away from the start).

The Situation:

  • Stack 2 wants to Push a new value.

  • It tries to move Top2 from 6 to 5.

  • Index 5 is occupied by the Queue. COLLISION!

  • The Stack reports "Stack Overflow" because it has hit the boundary of the Queue.

The Result:

  • The Stack cannot push.

  • HOWEVER, there are free blocks in memory at indices 0, 1, 2.

  • A Stack is a contiguous linear data structure. It cannot "skip" the Queue to use the free space at index 0.

This perfectly matches Option A: "you may not be able to add/push into the stack even when there are some free blocks in the memory."

Now we are replacing the Stack 1 with a circular queue, having two elements with front at index 0 and rear at index 1. Now enqueue 4 more elements in the queue resulting in rear pointing at index 5. Now push in the stack S2 so that all the spaces will be filled and S2 top pointing at index 6.

Suppose that we want to design a data structure called Mx-Queue that supports ONLY three operations as follows:

Enqueue(x) – It is a standard queue operation that equeue element x into the queue.

Dequeue() – It is a standard queue operation that dequeue from front of the queue.

FIND-MAX() – It is one extra operation that Mx-Queue supports which finds the maximum element from MX-Queue without removing it in $\mathrm{O}(1)$ time.

To fulfill the purpose we use one more auxiliary data structure along with a standard queue.

There are two choices of auxiliary data structures are available to us. (See figure for visual representation)

  • QueueStack
  • Queue

QueueStack is a data structure that has the special privilege of removing elements from the rear of the queue.

we call the following functions Insert() and Delete() to add or remove elements into or from Mx-Queue.

Insert(Mx-Queue,x): 
 Enqueue(Mx-Queue, X)
 //Do something with auxiliary data structure
End
Delete(Mx-Queue): 
 x = Dequeue(Mx-Queue)
 //Do something with auxiliary data structure
 Return x 
End

One of the Insert or Delete works in linear time and the other one works in constant time.

Choose the correct option.

  • $\text{S1}:$ We can implement Mx-Queue by using one Queue and QueueStack data Structure.
  • $\text{S2}:$ We can implement Mx-Queue by using two Queue data Structures.
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Based on the analysis of the data structures and the requirements for a Max-Queue, here is the step-by-step solution.

Understanding the Goal

We need to implement a queue that supports:

  1. Enqueue: $O(1)$ or $O(n)$

  2. Dequeue: $O(1)$ or $O(n)$

  3. Find-Max: $O(1)$ (Strict Requirement)

To find the maximum in $O(1)$ time, the auxiliary data structure must keep the maximum element accessible at all times (usually at the front). Since elements are added and removed, we typically use a technique called a Monotonic Decreasing Queue.

This technique maintains a list of potential maximum candidates in decreasing order. When a new element arrives, we remove all elements from the back of the auxiliary structure that are smaller than the new element (because the new element is "newer" and "larger," so the smaller ones will never be the maximum again).

Evaluating S1: Using Queue + QueueStack

A QueueStack (as defined in the image) supports:

  • Insert Rear

  • Delete Front

  • Delete Rear (The key feature)

Let's trace the Monotonic Queue algorithm with this setup:

Example: Enqueue 10, then 5, then 20.

  1. Enqueue(10):

    • Main Queue: [10]

    • Aux (QueueStack): [10]

  2. Enqueue(5):

    • Main Queue: [10, 5]

    • Aux (QueueStack): Compare 5 with Rear(10). 5 < 10. Just push 5.

    • Aux: [10, 5]

  3. Enqueue(20):

    • Main Queue: [10, 5, 20]

    • Aux (QueueStack): Compare 20 with Rear(5). 20 > 5. Delete Rear (5).

    • Compare 20 with Rear(10). 20 > 10. Delete Rear (10).

    • Push 20.

    • Aux: [20]

Result: The QueueStack allows us to "Delete Rear," which is essential to maintain the sorted order needed for $O(1)$ Find-Max.

  • Find-Max: Look at Front of Aux ($O(1)$).

  • Dequeue: Remove from Main. If the removed element matches Front of Aux, remove Front of Aux ($O(1)$).

  • Enqueue: Requires a loop to delete smaller elements, so it is worst-case $O(n)$ (though amortized $O(1)$).

Conclusion: S1 is correct.

Evaluating S2: Using Queue + Queue

A standard Queue supports:

  • Insert Rear

  • Delete Front

  • NO Delete Rear

Let's try the same example: Enqueue 10, then 5, then 20.

  1. Enqueue(10): Aux: [10]

  2. Enqueue(5): Aux: [10, 5]

  3. Enqueue(20):

    • We need to compare 20 with the elements at the rear. We see 5 is smaller than 20.

    • We want to remove 5. But a standard Queue cannot remove from the rear.

    • We cannot access 5 to remove it without first removing 10 (which is at the front). But 10 is the current maximum and must stay!

Because a standard Queue cannot delete the "newest" elements (Rear) while preserving the "oldest" elements (Front), it cannot maintain the monotonic decreasing property required to solve this problem efficiently.

Conclusion: S2 is incorrect.

Final Answer

Since we can implement the Mx-Queue using a QueueStack (Statement 1) but not using a standard Queue (Statement 2):

Correct Option:

A. S1 is correct but S2 is incorrect

Imagine four railroad cars positioned on the input side of the track in the figure below, numbered $1, 2, 3,$ and $4,$ from left to right. Suppose we perform the following sequence of operations (which is compatible with the direction of the arrows in the diagram and does not require cars to ”jump over” other cars):

  1. move car $1$ into the stack;
  2. move car $2$ into the stack;
  3. move car $2$ into the output;
  4. move car $3$ into the stack;
  5. move car $4$ into the stack;
  6. move car $4$ into the output;
  7. move car $3$ into the output;
  8. move car $1$ into the output.


As a result of these operations the original order of the cars, $1234,$ has been changed into $2431.$
If there are six railroad cars numbered $123456,$ Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: They can’t be permuted into the order $154623$
They can be permuted into the order $254613$
They can’t be permuted into the order $654123$
They can be permuted into the order $325641$

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

it is possible to obtain a permutation $p_1p_2\dots p_n$ from $12 \dots n$ using a stack if and only if there are no indices $i < j < k$ such that $p_j < p_k < p_i$

  • In (A), $p_5 < p_6 < p_2$ for indices $2 < 5 < 6.$
  • In (B), $p_5 < p_6 < p_2$ for indices $2 < 5 < 6.$ So,this permutation can’t be obtained.
  • In (C), $p_5 < p_6 < p_1$ for indices $1 < 5 < 6.$
  • In (D), To obtain $325641,$ do $\text{SSSXXSSXSXXX}$ where $\text{S}$ stands for ”move a
  • car from the input into the stack” and $\text{X}$ stands for ”move a car from the stack into the output.”

questions.qtext:
Suppose, you have proposed an optimal algorithm which uses extra stack(s) to design a stack such that $\textsf{GetMinimum()}$ should be $O(1)$ for n number of elements.

Consider the following statements:

  • $\text{S1} :$ Minimum number of extra stack(s) $: 1$
  • $\text{S2} :$ Time Complexity $: O(1)$
  • $\text{S3} :$ Space Complexity $: O(n)$

Which of the following is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 15)

Objective : To implement a stack such that, along with normal stack operations, it can perform GetMinimun() in O(1), we can use extra stack(s).

(We’ll try using only one extra stack (helper stack) to store current minimum for each element added)

push(x) –

  • First push(x) in original stack, also push(x) in helper stack.
  • For every subsequent push(x), check if x <= top() of helper stack. If x is lesser or equal, then push(x) in both stacks else push(x) only in original stack.

pop() –

  • temp = pop(), check if temp == top() of helper stack. If x is equal, then pop() from both stacks else do pop() from original stack only.
  • For last pop(), pop() from both stacks.

GetMinimum() –

  • return top() of helper stack.

We’ve successfully achieved our objective.

We’ve used only one helper stack. Thus, S1 is True.

Time complexity for GetMinimun(), push(), pop() is O(1). Thus, S2 is True.

In worst case, for every push(x) we’ve to also push(x) in helper stack. Thus, S3 is True.

Answer :- D.

Consider the following queue of characters, where QUEUE is a circular array which is allocated $6$ memory cells with indexing starting from $1.$
Consider the below status of Queue where Front and Rear stores $2$ and $4$ respectively.

Five sequences of operations have been performed on the current status of queue as described below.

  1. $\text{‘F’}$ is added to the queue
  2. Two items are removed
  3. $\text{‘K’, ‘L’}$ and $\text{‘M’}$ are added
  4. Two items are deleted
  5. $\text{‘R’}$ is added to the queue

What will be the final value of Front and Rear respectively?
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

n = size of queue = 6.

front = 1 rear = 3 ( considering 0 indexing in underlying array).

We’re performing 5 insert operations.

rear = ( rear + 5 ) mod 6 = 2.

We’re performing 4 remove operations.

front = ( front + 4 ) mod 6 = 5.

After operations, front = 5 and rear = 2.

This is in 0 indexing, so changing it back to 1 indexing will result in –

After operations, front = 6 and rear = 3

Answer :- D..
